reading.title: How Cities Keep Standing
reading.purpose: Learn how engineers inspect, repair, and redesign the hidden systems that keep a city running.
paras: Every morning, people turn on faucets, cross bridges, and flip light switches. Few stop to think about the infrastructure beneath their feet—the pipes, roads, bridges, and power lines that keep a town running. Behind the scenes, civil engineers check those systems each day.

Inspectors start by testing structural safety. They check how beams, walls, and posts hold up under heavy trucks and winter rain. Sometimes tree roots or gravel obstruct a storm drain, blocking water until streets flood. Clearing a small clog early costs far less than fixing a ruined street.

When a destructive storm hurts a public building, engineers first deconstruct the broken wall piece by piece. They want to see how the damage happened. Those close checks are deeply instructive, teaching teams which joints held strong and which parts wore out too soon.

Next, city planners ask people for constructive ideas—helpful notes meant to make the block better instead of just complaining. Neighbors might point out a dark crosswalk or a narrow ramp. Senior engineers also instruct newer crew members on updated safety rules before work starts.

Sometimes crews reconstruct a worn bridge in the same spot with stronger concrete. Other times, a growing town must restructure its transit plan, rearranging bus lanes and bike paths so riders stay safe. Building a city is never done. It is a steady loop of testing, learning, and fixing.

choices: made out of heavy concrete and thick steel beams
helpful and meant to improve a plan
damaged badly during a severe winter rainstorm
blocked by tree roots and gravel inside a drain

qs.q: Which sentence shows why engineers take apart a damaged wall carefully after a storm?
choices: Behind the scenes, civil engineers check those systems each day.
Clearing a small clog early costs far less than fixing a ruined street.
Those close checks are deeply instructive, teaching teams which joints held strong and which parts wore out too soon.
Sometimes crews reconstruct a worn bridge in the same spot with stronger concrete.
qs.why: This sentence explains that taking damaged parts apart teaches teams which joints lasted and which parts failed.

ev.text: Those close checks are deeply instructive, teaching teams which joints held strong and which parts wore out too soon.

qs.q: When would a town choose to restructure its transit plan instead of simply reconstructing one bridge?
choices: When the town has grown and needs a new arrangement of lanes and paths.
When tree roots have clogged a single storm drain along a quiet avenue.
When neighbors have no ideas to share about sidewalks or crosswalks.
When inspectors want to finish repairs without testing any concrete beams.
qs.why: Paragraph 5 contrasts rebuilding one bridge in place with a growing town rearranging bus lanes and bike paths.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Winter rain causes far more harm to city bridges than heavy trucks ever do.
Neighbors should clear gravel out of storm drains before every big storm.
Keeping a city working takes steady checking, learning, and fixing.
Civil engineers spend most of their time teaching newer workers safety rules.
qs.why: The reading explains how cities maintain infrastructure through testing, studying failures, listening to residents, and rebuilding or rearranging systems.
